If the government declines initially to provide its race-neutral reasons at step two, and the case is later remanded for further Batson proceedings, the government cannot offer brand-new justifications for its peremptory strike. We held as much in United States v. Taylor. There, we explained that “when ruling on a Batson challenge, the trial court should consider only the reasons initially given to support the challenged strike, not additional reasons offered after the fact.” 636 F.3d 901, 905 (7th Cir. 2011) (Taylor I) (citing Miller El II, 545 U.S. at 246–52). Similarly, in United States v. Brasher, we “declined to consider” the government’s newly provided rationale (there, on appeal) for striking a venireperson. 962 F.3d 254, 265 (7th Cir. 2020). “The problem with th[e government’s] explanation,” we held, was “that it was not voiced in the district court and instead was articulated for the first time on appeal.” Id. at 267. We agreed with the defendant “that the validity of the government’s peremptory challenges must stand or fall on the reasons provided to the district court during the Batson inquiry.” Id.

octen.title: Seventh Circuit Upholds Jury Selection Ruling in Batson Case | LAWS.com News
octen.snippet:
The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals recently ruled on a significant case concerning jury selection and racial discrimination. In the case of United States v. Andre Neal-Ford (Docket No. 20-2087), the court upheld a lower court's decision regarding the use of peremptory strikes against two jurors. This ruling is crucial as it impacts how courts evaluate claims of racial discrimination during jury selection, particularly in cases involving minority defendants.
The case arose from a criminal trial involving thirteen Black male defendants, where the government struck the only two non-white jurors from the jury panel. The defendants argued that this action violated their rights under the Equal Protection Clause, citing the landmark Supreme Court case, Batson v. Kentucky, which prohibits racial discrimination in jury selection. The Seventh Circuit had previously agreed with the defendants on this issue, leading to a remand for further examination of the jury selection process.
In the initial proceedings, the district court ruled that the defendants did not meet their burden of proving purposeful discrimination when the government used its peremptory challenges to strike Juror 26, a Black man, and Juror 58, a Hispanic woman. The defendants appealed, and the Seventh Circuit found that the district court had misapplied the Batson standard, specifically at the first step of the inquiry. The court remanded the case for a more thorough application of Batson's three-step process.
Upon remand, the district court revisited its analysis and held an evidentiary hearing.
